title: 650 commits later: a frog artillery game
author: TransportationOk5941
selftext:
This is Frog of War, a 2D artillery game where frogs blow up the terrain and each other (think Worms). I started it in mid February this year, and it's out on web, Android and iOS with online multiplayer, bots and a small cosmetic hat store.

Practically all of the code was written by Claude Code. I'm a developer by day, so I can read and review what it writes (which I did for a while, but I've pretty much stopped). This post is about how the way I work with it changed along the way, and how these experiences changed the following development. Hopefully it can help some of you out there.



# Weeks 1-6: vibes... pure vibes

The first six weeks were a sprint of about 350 commits. Day two already had destructible terrain, basic blocks shooting each other and a first attempt at multiplayer, because I wanted online play early.

Back then I still did the commits myself, so the messages said stuff like: "Got multiplayer working, sorta", "Got rid of multiplayer in order to reimplement", "Rewrote from HTTP to SignalR" and "Kni fix, probably". I ended up rebuilding multiplayer several times over before it held.

The game runs on Sharp2D, a small 2D engine of my own (built years ago, before AI) on top of KNI (a MonoGame fork which runs in the browser).

By the end of March it ran in the browser, on Windows, Android and iOS, and had a realtime mode next to the turn-based one.



# April to July: the break

For some reason I lost passion for it and barely touched it for three months, only about a dozen commits from mid-April to late July.



# July and August: the boring parts

When I came back I finally had the ambition to make it a real product: Google and Apple sign-in, coins, a hat store, Stripe on the web and in-app purchases on both stores. From the first store plan to purchases working on web, iOS and Android took about ten days. On my own I would never have bothered with that in a hobby project.

And yes, precisely 0 sales so far 😎



# Changing how I work with it

Around August the project got big enough that "just ask it" stopped working well. These are the changes that made the biggest difference: 

* \*Plans instead of prompts.\* One session works as an advisor. It reads the codebase and writes a self-contained plan with steps and stop conditions. A fresh session then executes that plan on its own branch. There are close to 30 plans now. Before building I let it grill me on the plan (one of Matt Pocock's skills), which catches most bad assumptions early. Definitely the most important step.
* \*One rule, one place.\* Most bugs in this project turned out to be the same rule written twice, once for singleplayer and once for the server, slowly drifting apart. AI is very happy to write a second copy of something that already exists. Now both call one implementation, and a test keeps them in sync. The project currently has about 1,450 tests.
* \*A doc per area.\* [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md) started as one file and kept growing. It's now short, and each area (simulation, weapons, multiplayer, HUD, audio and so on) has its own doc with its rules, including the "never do this" ones. Every task updates the doc it touches.



# Art and sound

Most of the newer sound effects are synthesized by a Node script it wrote. It renders a batch of candidates to a listening page, I pick the ones I like, and the script installs them. The HUD, map props and parts of the UI are drawn in canvas code and baked to PNGs by script.

For visuals I resorted to my ChatGPT subscription because I largely felt it did visuals better than Claude.

The background music for the menu and matches was generated with Suno.



# October and November: play-tests

The last two months were driven by play-tests: turn-costing bugs, a readable HUD, better aiming feedback, a fog of war rework and smarter bots. Plus new weapons, and most recently Rising Lava, which climbs in steps when a match drags on.



# Numbers

A bit under nine months, 651 commits, about 100k lines of C#, and clients for web, Windows, Android and iOS. Claude Code did practically everything, only some assets came from other platforms. It's free to play, the store only sells hats.

Web - [https://frogofwar.sogaardsoftware.com/game](https://frogofwar.sogaardsoftware.com/game)

Android - [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sogaardsoftware.frogofwar](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sogaardsoftware.frogofwar)

iOS - [https://apps.apple.com/us/app/frog-of-war/id6765942711](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/frog-of-war/id6765942711)



Happy to go deeper on any of it. If anyone wants to see what a plan or an area doc looks like, I can share one.

I'll also be hanging out in the multiplayer lobby for a few hours, if someone wants to play a few multiplayer matches 🎮
